Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

Welcome to payments

You're joining a team that processes transactions for millions of users.

Read the architecture doc in the wiki. Our three core services are the ledger (source of truth for account balances), the gateway (external payment processor integration), and the reconciliation job (catches divergence). Most backend work touches one of these. We optimize for correctness first, speed second.

Your first task is local development setup. The README in the payments repo has the steps. Run the full test suite when done—it should pass in under 2 minutes. If it doesn't, file an issue with the exact error and tag @backend-oncall. That signals a problem we need to fix. Tomorrow, read the last 10 merged pull requests to absorb our code style, naming conventions, and how we debate decisions. Open a PR with questions in the comments. We want you asking.

The payments integration tests run against a sandbox account with our processor, not mocks. You can verify your changes without risk to production.

This week, grab 2 hours on the calendar of whoever merges your first PR. You'll pair to learn the sharp edges directly—getting them wrong in production is expensive.

Add a section on who to ask for what.

Ledger questions go to @ledger-team. They own data consistency and can explain the balance calculation model. For performance tuning, ask them before optimizing queries—they've hit every wall.

Gateway integration issues are handled by @gateway-oncall. They know the nuances of each payment method and can debug transaction failures that don't reach our logs.

Reconciliation mismatches are @payments-data's domain. They own the job that catches divergence between our ledger and the processor, and can reconstruct a transaction's path if something doesn't reconcile. Database credentials and staging account access come from @platform-team—they run the sandbox, so tell them if you need to reset test data.

Read @payments-veterans on Slack when you have 15 minutes. That channel is where people post the gotchas they've hit—it's better than learning by hitting them yourself. If you're blocked and can't find the right person, post in #payments-general. Someone will point you to the right place within an hour.

Add a short note about the on-call rotation.

output: You'll join the on-call rotation in week three, after you've shipped your first few changes. The rotation is weekly, Monday through Sunday. On-call means you're the first person called if a payment system fails—it's urgent work. You'll carry a pager and have access to production logs and dashboards. The rotation schedule is in the wiki calendar. During your on-call week, avoid scheduling vacation or major refactors. When you rotate off, the next person takes over at 9 AM Monday. The team pays on-call premium for weeks where you're on duty. You'll learn how to diagnose failures fast—this is where you figure out what actually breaks.
